newsitem.title: MEXICO: New drug cartels mushroom across Mexico.
newsitem.headline: New drug cartels mushroom across Mexico.

text.p: New drug cartels have sprung up across Mexico, some of them shipping tonnes of narcotics to the United States and challenging the established Mexican gangs, a top law enforcement official said on Friday.

Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo, head of Mexico's National Institute for Drug Combat (INCD), told foreign correspondents smaller groups had mushroomed while authorities concentrated in the past on catching kingpins.
"We have detected that while the resources and the efforts are all directed against (capos) there are a series of smaller drug groups which are growing and growing each day," he said.

Mexico has three major drug trafficking organisations. The biggest is the Juarez cartel, run by Amado Carrillo Fuentes, nicknamed "Lord of the Skies" for flying in big shipments of Colombian cocaine for smuggling into the United States.

Carrillo this month gave police the slip in the northern state of Sinaloa, where he came on a hired jet for his sister's wedding. Agents were lying in wait but the capo received a tip-off that allowed him to escape in time.

The other two groups are the Gulf Cartel, whose leader Juan Garcia Abrego was convicted last October in a Texas court, and the Pacific cartel centred in the border city of Tijuana and led by the Arellano Felix brothers.

Although the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) says Carrillo has the biggest organisation, Gutierrez said the Juarez cartel probably had a smaller share of the total market than many people thought.

The new smaller cartels in some cases "ship tonnes rather than kilos" of narcotics and their combined traffic could be almost as big as that of the Juarez gang, he said. "So we now have to dismember the big cartels and stop the little groups from growing."
Gutierrez declined to say where the new groups were located, citing the confidentiality of investigations, but agreed the Yucatan peninsula "might be" one of the regions.

The fragmentation of Mexican drug trafficking into numerous smaller regional cartels reflects a similar tendency over the past few years in Colombia, where trafficking used to be dominated by Pablo Escobar's Medellin cartel and a rival gang based in Cali. But after police shot Escobar to death in 1993, the trade began to fragment into more than a score of "mini-cartels," many based in smaller provincial towns.
